subject: physics
question_text: What is gauge pressure? Describe how an open-tube manometer measures it.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 (Mechanical Properties of Fluids), Short Answer Question 3 (printed p.107). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: the full pressure at depth h below a free surface is P = P₀ + hρg; the gauge pressure is the hρg term alone, the amount by which P exceeds the atmospheric pressure P₀. An open-tube manometer is a U-tube with one arm open to the atmosphere and the other connected to the vessel, and the level difference h between its two arms gives P − P₀ = hρg directly; rearranging, h = (P − P₀)/ρg, so a lower-density liquid gives a taller, more readable column for a small pressure difference, and a higher-density liquid keeps the column short for a large one.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Gauge pressure defined
lines: by which the pressure at a
steps.margin_note: First mark. Give the definition, then the formula.
steps.why: Naming it a difference from atmospheric pressure, not the total pressure, is what separates gauge pressure from the pressure itself.
common_mistakes: Writing P_g = hρg without saying it equals P − P₀.
Calling P₀ the pressure at the point instead of the atmospheric pressure.

recall.must_convey: That gauge pressure is P minus P naught, equal to h rho g, the amount above atmospheric pressure.
accept: gauge pressure is h rho g

steps.memory_tip: Gauge pressure is the EXTRA over atmospheric — P minus P naught, not P itself.

steps.label: The open-tube manometer
lines: arm is open to the atmosphere,
and the other arm is connected
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Describe the device: a U-tube, one arm open, the other connected.
steps.why: The device works only because one arm is left open to a known pressure, atmospheric, so the other arm can be compared against it.
common_mistakes: Describing a closed tube with both ends sealed.
Leaving out which arm is open and which is connected to the vessel.

recall.must_convey: That an open-tube manometer is a U-tube with one arm open to air and the other connected to the vessel.
accept: one side open, one side connected

steps.memory_tip: One arm open to air, one arm to the vessel — that is the whole device.

steps.label: Reading the pressure difference
lines: levels in the two arms. The
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Say that the LEVEL DIFFERENCE h is what is read and used.
steps.why: The manometer converts a pressure difference, which cannot be seen, into a height difference, which can be measured with a scale.
common_mistakes: Reading the height of liquid in one arm alone instead of the difference between the two arms.
Using the density of the liquid inside the vessel instead of the density of the manometer liquid.

recall.must_convey: That the level difference h between the two arms gives P minus P naught equals h rho g.
accept: h rho g from the height difference

steps.memory_tip: Read the DIFFERENCE in level between the two arms, not either arm alone.

steps.label: Choice of liquid
lines: oil is used for small pressure
liquid such as mercury is used
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Name which liquid suits which range, and give the reason.
steps.why: For the same pressure difference, a smaller ρ gives a taller, easier-to-read column, while a larger ρ keeps the column short enough to fit a large difference on the same scale.
common_mistakes: Naming a liquid without saying which range, small or large, it suits.
Reversing the rule and saying mercury is used for small differences.

recall.must_convey: That a low-density liquid such as oil suits small pressure differences and a high-density liquid such as mercury suits large ones, because h is inversely proportional to ρ.
accept: oil for small, mercury for large
low density gives a taller column

steps.memory_tip: Small difference, small ρ (oil). Large difference, large ρ (mercury).

insider_note: The manometer turns a pressure difference into a height difference, and the fourth mark is choosing the right liquid density for the range being measured.
